comparison: For each active j, retain functions f_j, f_j-prime and f_j-double-prime with first-derivative relations for f_j and f_j-prime, and absolute bounds on all three uniformly over j in S and u in [0,1]. Within-domain derivatives allow the interval endpoint convention to be represented separately from unrestricted derivatives; do not demand a differentiable extension outside the interval without source support. Existence of the two derivatives is essential, since a total derivative operator equal to zero at nondifferentiable points would not assert it. Twice differentiability does not require continuity of the second derivative, so replacing the condition by C2 is stronger. The positive bounds are common across active components, not merely a separate finite constant for every j. No lower signal-strength bound follows, and inactive components are not automatically given pointwise zero representatives and derivatives by their L2 vanishing.

comparison: Retain a common positive lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue of every mode-k noise covariance and the stated resulting c*|S_m| lower bound for their sum. Individual positive definiteness with constants depending on l is weaker; the summed bound needs the elementary PSD-order argument rather than an assertion that eigenvalues add. A_epsilon,T here is the square T-by-T lag-covariance matrix with entries sum_(q>=0) a_q*a_(q+|t-s|), not the rectangular filter matrix sharing notation elsewhere. The scalar series must converge under the coefficient assumptions; a totalized real sum does not prove this. Keep y as the positive limit of min(d_k,T)/max(d_k,T), y-star=min(y,1), and c1 in the left-open, right-closed interval (1-y-star,1]. The eigenvalue lower bound is at one-based index floor(c1*T), for large T, and is strict above positive c2. Translate to zero-based Fin indexing only after proving that index lies in 1,...,T eventually; this is a positive spectral-quantile bound, not necessarily a smallest-eigenvalue bound unless c1=1.
